commenti.body: He's in so many things. Also loved him in About Time, Anna Karenina, Black Mirror, and the Patient. He does tend to play quiet/sweet characters, most of the time, but I don't think ALL of his roles are like that so I don't think he's necessarily just playing himself.
Thanks! Good to know. I want to watch Ex Machina tonight if I can stop working. Will come back with some thoughts.

Most commercially viable actors play mostly the same type of characters most of the time. It’s very easy to notice once you start watching a bunch of films with the same person.

It’s not about being typecast, it’s just about the same kind of subspecialisation you see in any career. Casting directors like to know what they’re getting and the more an actor plays a specific way the better they get at it.

Truly versatile leads and character actors are a very small minority of working actors.

Interesting, thanks for that! What you said reminds me as well how once actors become a certain age that they begin character acting roles. I believe 2015 was a year that was transformative for Gleeson with Brooklyn, Star Wars: The Force Awakens, The Revenant and Ex Machina all getting Oscar nominations. I suppose I'd like to see a more challenging role but even our favourites have their own will.

He's one of the few modern actors that I'll go out of my way to watch. I feel like he's often typecast as a creep or a weirdo, like his role in the new Star Wars trilogy (which is a major highlight of those movies), his role in The Patient, and The Little Stranger. But he's also able to play a likeable, normal guy, like his role in Black Mirror. It a shame that he wasn't able to play a more substantial Weasley. Such a thing would've elevated some of those Harry Potter movies.

At times, directors leverage the feelings evoked from previous roles not simply for drawing on unconscious associations, but as part of what they explore with their art.  

 If we bring our preconceptions about what type of person Domnall Gleason plays into Ex Machina, it's possible we might interpret the film differently than if we don't.  I'm interested in what you thought of the film.

Thanks for asking!

Directors are using performances as a springboard, or trampoline? Good call. On second watch of Ex Machina, listening for cues in the dialogue between both Caleb and Nathan and Ava and Caleb, Domhnall Gleeson must depict an impressionable young man as Caleb. He is entirely reactionary. Alex Garland could have used sketches of Gleeson's John in Lenny Abrahamson's Frank, with a childlike quality, and willingness to trust while these are elements of demeanour over the "reality" of the characters, e.g. the social media narrative voice of John in Frank, creating content on the making of music becoming performative as the result, the actual art is unremarkable, whereas Caleb is repeatedly asked his opinion of Ava, the inquisitor being Nathan, not for his technical opinion [Caleb's technical opinion is unremarkable to Nathan as Nathan is established as a computational genius]. Caleb's state of suggestibility is highlighted as the conversation over the Jackson Pollock painting is the turning point for him, he decides [or is directed] to go with his emotions. He never appears to take agency or overview. Both Caleb and John remind me that the principle reasoning for creating public education is that children are required to be socialised. Caleb and John enter into the worlds of their deutoragonists and foils like one enters primary, or elementary school. Using both for this entry level schooling is to call on the status of the characters spiritual awakening. Are they adaptive, experiencing Awakening in midlife [making reference to Strauss & Howe], having survived Crisis in youth? Are they Idealist & Reactive? 

In Frank, John takes agency [and awakens] by acting to repair the relationship between Frank and his band while Caleb suffers the consequence of not taking agency [possibly to live another day or not]. He is Ava's test and she has passed. The two characters have differing results in a hopeful vs dystopian foray.

I might at some point, but something about the idea of it doesn't inspire me. I could check it in a few years or watch them with my adult kids to catch what they think of them. I think after John Boyega's experience in The Force Awakens, I kind of got the ick.
